description: Golden table for keyboard occlusion on interaction tap points (#2589), consumed by packages/contracts/src/tap-keyboard-occlusion.ts. A visible software keyboard is its own system surface: it is never a covering sibling of app content, so the same-window occlusion classifier cannot see it, and it leaves the app window rect intact, so the viewport rule passes a covered tab bar. The band runs from the topmost keyboard node down to the bottom of the viewport, across the keyboard's own columns; the tap point is the point the interaction dispatches: the rect center the platform aims at for a ref handed over by name, or the touch point a parent with interactive descendants resolves instead. `nodes` are captured snapshot nodes as they appear in the projection the interaction resolved against — note that regular and interactive projections prune the keyboard's own container, leaving Key nodes beside app chrome. Three rules decide whether reported geometry may be measured at all. Docking: the band is derived only where the keyboard's own reported geometry reaches the viewport's bottom edge within 80 units — measured on iPhone 17 Pro (26.2) the reported key plane stops 58 pt short of an 874 pt portrait viewport and lands exactly on a 402 pt landscape one, and on iPad Pro 11-inch (M4) 3 pt short of a 1210 pt viewport — so an iPad floating keyboard, an app-drawn keypad, or an IME that stops above its own navigation bar stays unmeasured and fails open. The budget is counted in the same units as the rects it guards, which is what a measured Android IME asks for rather than what a dp table would give: with three-button navigation on Pixel 7 (Android 16, 1080x2400 at 420 dpi), Gboard's reported region runs to the physical display bottom at 2400 while the 126 px navigation bar occupies 2274..2400 inside it, so no Android keyboard measured so far needs slack for the bar. Width: geometry that comes back taller than it is wide did not arrive in the app's orientation space — iOS reports the landscape iPhone keyboard in the keyboard's own rotated space — and is refused measurement for the same reason. Tiling: the keys themselves must form one unbroken run of columns, because a split iPad keyboard docks both clusters at the bottom edge while its surface container still spans the whole screen, and the app content between the clusters is visible and tappable. Reported seams are zero on every measured tree — iPhone 17 Pro's reported row adjoins across 395 pt, iPad Pro 11-inch's across 743.5 pt, and Gboard's across 1070 px — so the allowance covers rounding rather than layout, and a gapped band is refused measurement like the two above. That rule is deliberately blunt in both directions, and the last two cases name the trade: a sparse layout such as the iOS emoji panel reports corner keys over a wide container, does not tile, and reads `undetermined` — the guard abstains there rather than inventing which gaps are app content; and a projection that reports the container with no keys at all has nothing left to check, so the band is the container's own claim. Every captured iOS and Android keyboard measured so far reports its keys, so the second shape is the harness's, not a captured one. `target` names either a resolved node index or a bare coordinate point; both paths read one decision and choose their own consequence. A case that reaches a band declares its whole shape — the frame the refusal and the disclosure both quote, and the control rects that excuse a bare coordinate, which is where plane exclusion shows up.

the band reaches the viewport bottom, so a target in the unreported home-indicator strip is refused too
an element only partly under the keyboard keeps tapping: the rule is the center, not the overlap
a tap point exactly on the band's top edge is on the keyboard, not above it
a key the caller named is the tap they meant, so the keyboard never blocks its own keys
the key plane itself is keyboard-owned as well
app chrome flattened to the same parent as the keys stays app content
Android input method window owns the band by package provenance
an IME-owned node the caller named is not occluded by its own window
a window offset below the display origin measures the band against its own bottom edge
a narrow keyboard owns only its own columns, so app content beside it keeps tapping
a bare coordinate behind the keyboard reads the same decision the element path gets
a bare coordinate landing on a key is the keyboard the caller asked for
a bare coordinate inside the reported key plane but on no key is still the keyboard, not app content
a bare coordinate below the reported key plane still lands on the keyboard
an element whose center sits on a key is refused even though that coordinate alone would pass
no keyboard in the tree means nothing to refuse
an app-drawn keypad that stops short of the bottom edge is not the system keyboard's band
keyboard nodes with no usable rect leave the band unmeasurable, which fails open
no viewport leaves the band's bottom edge unknowable, which fails open
the keyboard dock's own button is the keyboard, not app content waiting behind it
an app control sharing the dock strip's band with the keyboard is still refused
a bare coordinate landing on the keyboard dock's button is the keyboard the caller asked for
the landscape iPhone keyboard reports its rects in its own rotated space, which cannot be measured
a landscape keyboard reported wide and docked is measured against the landscape viewport
the reported key plane stops above the home-indicator strip and the band still owns that strip
an iPad floating keyboard is not docked, so the band stays unmeasured and the tap fails open
an iPad split keyboard whose clusters stop above the docking budget is refused measurement by the docking rule first
a bottom-anchored app keypad wearing the keyboard types owns its band, which is the rule's accepted trade-off
a zero-area viewport leaves the band bottom edge unknowable, which fails open
a measured iPad keyboard docked at the bottom owns the strip below its reported keys
a split iPad keyboard docked at the bottom reports two clusters, and the gap between them is not the keyboard's to measure
Gboard reports its region down to the physical display bottom, across a 126 px three-button navigation bar
